content: Trypan Blue is a sterile ophthalmic solution containing an acid diazo group dye. It is primarily used during ophthalmic surgical procedures, such as vitrectomy, to selectively stain epiretinal membranes (ERM) and internal limiting membranes (ILM) in the human eye. This staining facilitates the identification and removal of these membranes during surgery. The solution is composed of trypan blue, sodium chloride (NaCl), and water for injection, with an osmolality range of 257-314 mOsm/kg. The solution is indicated for use in ophthalmic surgery to stain epiretinal membranes, aiding in their removal. It is contraindicated when a non-hydrated (dry state), hydrophilic acrylic intraocular lens (IOL) is planned for insertion, as the dye may be absorbed by the IOL and cause staining. Common adverse reactions include discoloration of high-water-content hydrogen intraocular lenses and inadvertent staining of the posterior lens capsule and vitreous face. These effects are generally self-limited and resolve within one week. Before use, the syringe must be primed to ensure smooth plunger movement. This involves retracting the plunger or twisting it clockwise into the stopper until tight, then continuing to rotate it until the stopper moves freely within the syringe. The syringe is then ready for injection. During administration, care must be taken to avoid contact between the cannula and the retina to prevent damage. Sufficient staining is expected upon contact with the membrane, and all excess dye should be removed from the vitreous cavity before performing an air-fluid exchange to prevent unnecessary spreading of the dye. Trypan Blue can also be injected directly into a balanced salt solution (BSS)-filled vitreous cavity instead of under air. Clinical use has demonstrated that sufficient staining is achieved after 30 seconds of application under BSS following complete vitreous and posterior hyaloid removal. Trypan Blue is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, indicating that it has shown teratogenic effects in animal studies, including neural tube, cardiovascular, vertebral, tail, and eye defects, as well as increased post-implantation mortality and decreased fetal weight. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and it should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. It is not known whether Trypan Blue is excreted in human milk, so caution should be exercised when administering it to nursing mothers. The safety and effectiveness of Trypan Blue have been established in pediatric patients, supported by evidence from well-controlled studies. No significant differences in safety and effectiveness have been observed between elderly and younger patients. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in relation to gender, race, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. Trypan Blue has been shown to be carcinogenic in rats and mutagenic in the Ames test, causing DNA strand breaks in vitro. Limited information is available regarding its pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and postmarketing experience. The solution is stored at 15-25°C (59-77°F) and should be protected from direct sunlight. There is no established interaction between Trypan Blue and alcohol, and patients are advised to consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while using this medication.
